utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. Today was scheduled to have the pre-Defence conference. The Chamber received two motions last Monday: One motion to stay the proceedings, and one motion for further time to prepare for the Defence. The Chamber has decided that we'll start to hear these motions today. The Chamber was unpleasantly surprised by the fait accompli it was confronted with last Monday. But before I give an opportunity to the parties to make any further oral submissions on the motions, there are a few matters pending which I would like to briefly address. The first one being that the Prosecution would inform the Chamber on the results of any discussions regarding the use of the words, and I quote, "or other non-Serb populations" in the indictment. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just to recap briefly: I don't believe there was any significant gap in understanding between the Defence and the Prosecution on that matter. The Court just accorded the Prosecution additional time to review the indictment to see if there are any references to "non-Serb populations" that the exclusion of which would render that portion of the indictment somehow difficult to understand. And we didn't find such references. So we think the understanding reached earlier addressing the nature of the charges of persecution, for example, directed against the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat populations and the exclusion of the other non-Serb populations stands. So unless the Defence has any additional questions about the meaning of that, and I don't believe it does, I think -- we appreciate the additional time provided by the Court, but no further clarification appears necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Fine. Thank you. Mr. Krajisnik, I saw that you were raising your hand. I do not know what you wanted to address at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to say good morning to the Trial Chamber. Secondly, I have appealed the decision on my defence, and I don't know whether it has been put on the agenda and whether I will be given an opportunity to say something on that item of the agenda, which is closely connected to what you have just mentioned. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, you say that you have appealed the decision, the decision on which the Chamber decided that you would not be unrepresented. The Chamber is aware that you did send a letter to the Trial Chamber. We'll deal with that letter at a later stage this morning. But perhaps it's good to say already that your observation that you have appealed the decision might be wrong. But we'll deal with that at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I observe: This case is full of unpleasant surprises, and one unpleasant surprise for the Defence is to hear at this moment that a letter has been sent to the Trial Chamber which has never been communicated to us, notwithstanding specific discussion in the past on the topic of information being transmitted immediately to the Defence when received in such circumstances by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When we deal with the matter later this morning, one of the issues will be that the Chamber would not further receive this kind of direct communication. I was not fully aware -- the letter reached the Chamber recently in translation. If you are not aware of the letter, I was not aware that -- then of course I'll take care that it will be distributed. I take it, as a matter of fact, that once you have seen it and once the Chamber has addressed the matter, that you might be satisfied with the way the Chamber has dealt with it. If not, of course, there will be another opportunity to give any -- make any observations you'd like. But the Chamber is confident that counsel will be satisfied with the way the Chamber deals with the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm happy to hear that confidence, Your Honour, and I'm sure I shall make my judgement when I see that material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. First of all, the entire appeal was sent to my Defence on a CD. Secondly, I kindly ask you to allow me to appeal against the decision. I have addressed the Trial Chamber on a number of occasions. I have addressed the Registry as well. I've asked for legal help to help me put the appeal together. This is the appeal to my submission, not to a submission by my Defence, and hence the difference, and the difference is major here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll deal with the matter at a later stage, Mr. Krajisnik. Perhaps for the moment it will be sufficient to remind you that this Chamber has decided that you are represented by counsel and that the Registry has informed you that it will not assign any additional legal expertise where counsel is already assigned to you. We'll deal with the matter at a later stage. The next issue on the agenda is that the Defence was expected to give its position on the issue of the testimony of Davidovic. You certainly remember the issue related to that. That was during the week of the 3rd of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say -- I'm sorry. I beg your pardon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was linked to the start of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must confess, I'm completely unaware that any such direction was given in relation to this matter. I certainly don't forget the matter. Your Honour can be absolutely sure I'll never forget it. But I really am unaware of any such direction having been given. What I remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it was discussed, I don't know exactly when, but it was discussed when we would receive the position of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't remember that either, Your Honour, to be to be absolutely frank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: During the next break, I'll find exactly where it was said and just to remind you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If it was, Your Honour, indeed. If anything was said on that point, not just where it was said but whether it was said as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, if it was said nowhere, I would not be in a position, of course, to tell you when it was said. But the Chamber - that's at least my recollection - linked it to the beginning of the Defence case. Since we'll have to adapt some of the scheduling anyhow, the Chamber would not insist on receiving it on a date as is in my recollection. But let's deal with it after the first break and then exactly find the moment on which anything was said on the timing of the findings of the Davidovic matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So we're leaving item 2, then, for the moment, are we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the moment. Perhaps we'll come back to it after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour, that's helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the next item on the agenda is the Chamber would like to give an opportunity, as requested, to the Defence and of course also then to the Prosecution to make any further submissions on the motion to stay. We'll split up the hearing of the motions, first the motion to stay and then the moment for extension of time. Mr. Stewart. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm dealing with this motion, Your Honour. I can be extremely brief, because matters are set out fully in the short motion, because the point is short, but we submit an important one nonetheless. Could I first of all contend that no analogy should be drawn from this application for a stay with that which sometimes follows an application for a stay following a motion that is rejected by the Chamber, certification then granted. The difference here, as I hope both the application for the stay makes clear, and also the appeal document itself, this, we contend, is an automatic right of appeal pursuant to Rule 108, this being an issue of a judgement of acquittal. And therefore, whilst in normal circumstances a Chamber would be very reluctant to grant a stay following the rejection of a motion, as I've already said, here the situation, I contend, is quite different. And we would invite particular caution on the part of the Chamber before allowing the case to be proceed any further. In principle, we submit, it's wrong to say to an accused that that accused needs to start putting up his defence when there is a chance, through an appeal procedure, an appeal procedure as of right, we would emphasise, that he may not have to put up a defence because his appeal might be accepted in whole or in part. For this purpose, we contend, it doesn't really matter whether the appeal is accepted in whole or in part. The situation is identical. The accused would be forced, were no stay granted, to put up a defence when in due course it transpires as a result of a decision of the Appeals Chamber he need not have done so. Additionally, again, as I hope the motion makes clear, practically it is unfair on the Defence in general where uncertainty exists over which part of the indictment may or may not be struck out following the appeal, to say that the accused has to answer the whole of the indictment. The argument is simple. Until such time as the accused knows which part of the indictment he does ultimately have to face, it's unfair to expect him to have to call evidence in relation to the whole indictment. It's going to affect the spread of time that the accused has, the choice of witnesses, so on and so forth, all the various matters that will in due course need to be considered by the Defence, the Prosecution, and indeed the Chamber in the 73 ter conference. Your Honour, I'd also invite this Chamber not to underestimate what is said in paragraphs 9 and 10 of the motion, and I'm going to deal with this extremely briefly, because it wasn't that long ago. It was the 16th of August, I think, that I addressed this Chamber on this very issue. Rule 98 bis, as we know, was amended during the course of this trial. As the Court is aware, it was the Defence submission that that amendment was fundamental to the operation of Rule 98 bis. In effect, as of course is its right, the Trial Chamber disagreed with that submission, rejected it, and we contend that the matter requires resolution by the Appeals Chamber. If the Defence are right that Rule 98 bis, when amended, was amended in a fundamental way, and if the Defence are right that as a result of that, prejudice - and we say severe prejudice - was caused to the accused, it is possible, we would submit more than possible, that relief sought in the appeal document may be granted in part or in whole. The result of that is that this Chamber would be ordered, in effect, return to the 98 bis stage and reconsider the matter on the basis of a motion and reconsider the matter, if I could put it again in the way that I did at the time, line by line, item by item, in the very schedules. Well, Your Honour, I needn't say that were that to happen in the middle of the Defence case, then the situation would be totally untenable and utterly absurd. And we submit that in those circumstances there would be a very real chance that the trial would actually not just degenerate into farce, but the trial may actually end up having to be aborted simply because at that particular juncture, so much of the Defence case would have been heard. That may well have related to things that were then struck out as a result of the return to 98 bis motion, and on top of that, there's every chance the Defence will be contending, well, how can this Chamber reconsider a full 98 bis motion when it had heard half of the Defence case? It's a very real and severe practical problem. In our submission, bearing in mind, to go back to the point that I've begun with, the accused has an appeal as a right from a Rule 98 bis ruling, bearing in mind how fundamental it is, as fundamental as anything that comes before the Trial Chamber or the Appeal Chamber, namely, the issue of judgement of acquittal. We submit that in reality, a trial logically should proceed in stages. The stage that we have reached is that this Chamber has ruled in relation to our 98 bis submission, which in our submission was not a motion, as is made clear in the document, in the Appeal Chamber document. And we submit finally that following that through logically, to allow the case to proceed until the matter has been resolved by the Appeal Chamber, one way or the other, would not only be unfair but would be impractical and could lead to absurdity. In our submission, the only course of action that is open to this Chamber at this stage is to grant the relief sought, to order a stay, as awkward and impractical as that might be to the proceedings and allow the Appeal Chamber to resolve the matter, and thereafter for the trial to continue, if the Appeal Chamber finds that the accused has a case to answer, in whole or in part, or of course the Appeal Chamber might order a return to the 98 bis stage, as I've already mentioned. Those are the submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, before I give an opportunity to the Prosecution, I'd like to receive a clarification on one of the issues. You say it is not only absurd and impractical, but -- and illogical, but it's also prejudicial to the accused if the 98 bis procedure would be revisited after we would have heard portions of the evidence presented by the Defence. I'm trying to understand that. Would that mean that -- let's just assume -- I'm not saying that it is a real possibility, but it's for the Appeals Chamber to decide. Let's just assume that the Appeals Chamber would instruct this Trial Chamber to go through the 98 bis procedure again. If we would have heard, apart from whether we could separate that in our minds, but let's just also assume that it would influence us in one way or another to have heard evidence which favours the Defence case. How could that be prejudicial to a decision to be taken under 98 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of course, it assumes that the evidence will in fact favour the Defence case. I mean, clearly we will endeavour to call evidence that is going to favour our case. But like any sensible counsel, we appreciate that our witnesses are going to face cross-examination. That cross-examination will no doubt be testing, and that may well affect matters firstly, in my submission. Secondly, witnesses will have to address issues presently in relation to the indictment as set out. If the indictment is in some way changed, either by the Appeal Chamber or by revisiting of 98 bis by this Chamber, then, in my submission, there is real prejudice to the Defence if there is called evidence which has then no place or status in the trial thereafter. In an adversarial system, and I appreciate this is a hybrid system, in an adversarial system it really can't be fair to invite a party to call evidence when there is a real chance that that evidence is evidence it need not have called as a result of a further ruling by a higher body, namely, the Appeal Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have nothing more to add, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This comes back, of course, to the potential of the Trial Chamber to separate and to select what evidence. Because if you say we've heard perhaps some evidence given during cross-examination which, although we expect the evidence to be presented to be in favour of the accused, that there is a possibility that there would be evidence which would be adverse to the Defence case, then we are more or less in the same situation, isn't it, as we are when we have seen some evidence which needs to be excluded for -- and which we have to bend from our minds. Isn't that one of the elements of this hybrid system?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, it may be one of the elements. In fairness to the Defence, it isn't the only submission on this point. It's also, as I've already said, the balance that we give to that particular issue, an issue which in due course might play no more part in the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand you understand your point. Mr. Harmon or Mr. Tieger, because we have not put on the record who are here, but at least it was Mr. Stewart for the Defence and Mr. Josse, and I see Mr. Harmon and Mr. Tieger being present for the Prosecution. Would you like to respond to motion -- the motion to stay?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. And I hope my response will be brief. The question raised by the Court to the Defence in connection with the issue of prejudice is one that I had wished to focus on, and I think the questions and responses largely tend to obviate that. I would simply note that our position is that there is no prejudice of the type and nature described by the Defence. I find, actually, that that's exemplified in the Defence motion itself when its emphasis seems to be at the early stage of the motion that the problem is the impression, and I'm quoting when I use that term, "upon Mr. Krajisnik and the general public of pre-emption of the judgement if this were to go forward." That's a far cry from actual prejudice that is really at the subject of such motions. The Defence raises a number of essentially illusory difficulties. I think the Court's question has illustrated that. Mr. Josse refers to the Defence position that in an adversarial system proceeding in this manner would be unfair. I think more accurately what underlies Mr. Josse's point would be in a jury system. And the Defence ignores the fact that this is not a system in which it's incumbent upon the procedure to keep from jurors the kind of evidence that may be excluded from them in the course of adversarial systems where juries are the finders of fact. As the Court has noted, here we have professional Judges who are called upon on a daily basis to make such distinctions and who are clearly capable of making such distinctions in this particular case. I would note further in emphasising the illusory nature of the Defence concerns about prejudice that there was no contention by the Defence that any of the counts of the indictment would fall. The thrust of the current motion is whether or not any of the supporting evidence underlying those counts might at some point be excluded from the case. The thrust of the Defence case is clearly not going to be an effort to combat or dispute or contest incidents or events about which they claim the Prosecution has produced no evidence. It's very clear that the thrust of the Defence case will be elsewhere, will not be focussed on incidents that were not raised during the course of the Prosecution case. So I would simply note that, finally, that the practical difficulties that the Defence seems to cite simply don't exist here, and -- which is precisely the reason, we would submit, the Defence declined to engage in a line-by-line review of the evidence produced in the case, a line-by-line review of the indictment. I would remind the Court that was a Defence decision. They declined to do so. Largely, we would submit, because the practical effect was minimal, if not non-existent. And there's no basis for the contention that any prejudice would result here from proceeding. Quite the contrary; there's, we would submit, prejudice from not proceeding in a variety of ways. The case needs to move forward. And that even in the unlikely event that some aspects of the evidence supporting the counts of the indictment were to be excluded from the case, its pragmatic impact on the case would be essentially non-existent and there is no potential prejudice from moving forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Josse, the first time you heard a response from the Prosecution, so if you'd like to briefly respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I will be very brief, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll have an opportunity to do to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I first of all say that we do not accept what Mr. Tieger says at line 18, 19 of page 12, that the Defence declined to engage in a line-by-line review of the evidence for that very reason. He sets out at that particular part of his submission. We simply don't accept that as being an accurate reflection of the situation. Could I also make one other correction to what Mr. Tieger has said. He cites the top of page 3, part of paragraph 6 of the Defence motion. What he fails to point out is that paragraph 6 in fact, and I'm not going to read it out. The first three lines deal with a particular point and he failed to mention the words even leaving aside the substantive issue. So the point being made about the impression is purely a subsidiary one, it's not the main point, and for Mr. Tieger to say that gives the game away, the Defence using the words the impression upon Mr. Krajisnik, is simply a misreading, in our submission, of paragraph 6 of the actual motion. Your Honour, Mr. Tieger makes the point that the Defence are alluding to what the situation would be in a jury system. We firmly reject that submission. We are very aware that this is not a jury system. We are very aware that this is a hybrid system. And we appreciate that it's Your Honour and Your Honour's colleagues who are in due course going to resolve all the issues in this case, both legal and factual. But that does not mean to say that any of the Judges of this or any other court are robots. It also does not mean to say that one shouldn't proceed with caution. It also doesn't mean to say that some of the fundamental matters that apply in an adversarial trial in this regard do not apply here. Of course there are significantly different considerations to a jury trial. We accept that. But we do not accept what Mr. Tieger says, that realistically we're trying to make a point that would be applicable in a jury system but not in a system where there is trial by judge rather than jury. No, Your Honour. We submit strongly that the point is equally good in this type of system as it would be in a jury system. One final point. So far as material is concerned that witnesses may or may not come up with, these are Defence witnesses from the witness-box, of course if those witnesses are dealing with matters which in due course they would not have needed to have dealt with, the Prosecution, as well as the Chamber, as well as the public in general, would have heard things that they otherwise would not have heard, material that the Prosecution might be able to use and material, we submit, that may leave some impression on the Chamber, despite no doubt its best efforts to remove such impression and evidence from its mind. Finally, I contend, Your Honour, that, for whatever reasons, perhaps because he thinks it's a very bad point, Mr. Tieger did not address points 9 and 10 in the Defence motion, which we, as I've already said, do place very strong reliance upon. We do say that were we right, were the Defence submission at the 98 bis hearing to be the correct one, rather than the ruling of the Chamber, and were the Appeal Chamber to agree with the Defence, to return in detail to the 98 bis stage by way of motion and the old rule would simply be almost an impossibility, if not an impossibility, were we in the middle of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. The Chamber considers it the best way of proceeding to first see whether we can reach a decision, whether that would be already a fully reasoned decision is not a matter on the motion to stay. Because if that motion would be decided, then we would not have to continue on the basis of assumptions. But of course if we would not reach a final decision, then the Chamber nevertheless prefers to continue on the basis of what observations the parties would like to make on the other motion, just in case the Chamber would deny the motion to stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, while I'm on my feet, but really it's for Mr. Stewart to deal with. As indeed the stay motion made clear, our preferred course was for judgement on the stay motion before proceeding. But the agenda yesterday made clear the situation, and of course we don't and can't -- perhaps I should put it the other way around. We can't and don't argue with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, we'll take some time to see whether we can finally decide on the first motion. If so, we'll deliver the decision and we'll then proceed. If not, we'll let the parties know and we'll invite the parties to proceed on the assumption that what should be said in case the motion would be denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As I've already said, Mr. Stewart is aware of that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we adjourn, Mr. Krajisnik, it appears to us that you have not informed counsel about the letter you addressed to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I interrupt? I think I need to make this clear. I saw Mr. Krajisnik at the UNDU yesterday, and without in any way waiving privilege, he informed me and Mr. Karganovic. Unfortunately, we were unable, through no fault of Mr. Krajisnik's, to remove the disk which contained the material. So we have not seen it and it was yesterday that he informed us. Perhaps I should also add: He had alluded to the fact that he either had done this or was going to do this. It was a little uncertain to me in the past week or so. But it was yesterday he told me in terms about his dealings both with the Chamber and indeed some dealings with the Registry. So could I put that on the record?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's fine. But at the same time, I can imagine that you'd like to have a copy of the translation of the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Very much so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'd just like to add, Your Honour, at risk of doing a double act, there's no conflict between us. But in the course of an extremely busy day, that information was transmitted to me by Mr. Josse. But we had a meeting with the Registry as well, and my position at the end of the day was I was unable to ascertain exactly what had gone to the Registry. I knew something had gone to the Registry, but they had not passed it on to me. That has been a topic of discussion, to try to reach some sensible understanding between the Registry about transmission. I had actually -- for whatever reason, I had no idea that Mr. Krajisnik had been in direct contact with the Trial Chamber. It was slightly unclear to me whether he had actually filed or not, and in fact it was unclear to the representative of the Registry in the discussion yesterday. So that's the position. But I didn't have any idea that he had been in direct contact with the Trial Chamber, Your Honour. I did know he had been in some contact with the Registry but I had not seen the material and I did not myself see Mr. Krajisnik yesterday because, well, we can't do everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understand. Perhaps in order to make matters even more complex, I do understand that further correspondence was addressed to the Appeals Chamber. A copy, as far as I understand, being sent to the Trial Chamber. I have not seen the content. I just know that there is such correspondence. The Chamber still will have to decide whether it's of any use to read copies of correspondence addressed to the Appeals Chamber, not through counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: To the Trial Chamber or Appeals Chamber, Your Honour? Now I'm getting even more confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that it's -- from what I understood, it was addressed to the Appeals Chamber and that a copy was sent to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for your information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for half an hour, and you'll learn after this break whether the Chamber was able to reach a decision on the motion to stay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber apologises for having taken a bit more time, but finally it preferred to see whether it could present a decision to the parties rather than to leave them in uncertainty. Therefore, I will first give a decision on the motion, the Defence motion, to stay. The motion is denied, and a written decision will follow. And the Chamber tries to do its utmost best to file that written decision still this afternoon. Then the next point on the agenda is that the Chamber gives an opportunity to the parties to make further oral submissions on the motion for extension of time. And perhaps, but I'm looking at you, Mr. Stewart. You specifically asked for oral argument. Do you think that it would be of any use to already know what the initial response of the Prosecution would be so that you can take that into account if you make further oral submissions, or would you consider the oral submissions you have in mind of such a character that we should rather wait to give an opportunity for the Prosecution to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it would probably be a quite helpful to hear what the Prosecution had to say, but it occurs to me, it is a question of what Your Honours have in mind. Because it seems quite likely that some things I say will lead the Prosecution to wish to say something else. If they are perhaps two bites in that way, that might be quite helpful, but I'm in Your Honour's hands. It's not a big issue for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This observation certainly assisted. Mr. Tieger, or Mr. Harmon, would it be a good idea that you briefly respond to the motion at this moment so that at least the Defence knows what your position is, and that if anything to be submitted at a later stage by the Defence would trigger any need to further respond, that we'll give an opportunity to you later?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, it remains to be seen precisely how helpful that will be, Your Honour, but I'm happy to provide some preliminary response and guidance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That would be essentially as follows: The Prosecution submits, number one, that the test that the Defence appears to be urging the Court to use in determining this motion is unsupported by any jurisprudence or case-law. We find that the -- essentially that the factual underpinnings for this particular motion have been raised on previous occasions and addressed by the Court, and in that respect, the Prosecution does not find any change of circumstance or underlying basis for the motion which would justify any departure from or deviation from the Court's previous orders. We also intended to note at least one of the specific aspects of the motion. That was the Defence's reference to or acknowledgment of the accused's failure to make the required financial contribution. Without belabouring that point at this stage, we would simply note that the impact of $180.000 of legal services on the ability to produce an exhibit list and a 65 ter list is immense, and I think it's very clear that at a minimum, one would expect that the 65 ters would have been completed and that indeed the remainder of the deficit between where the Defence says it now stands and what the Court order was would have been bridged. So that's fundamentally our position in response. I don't know if I've omitted any particular detail that might have been of greater assistance to the Defence in making its current argument or might have narrowed the issues which it needs to address, and I'm happy to respond to any questions the Court might have, but I trust that provides a sufficient insight into the Prosecution's position on the motion generally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I must say straight away, that is helpful. It's extremely helpful to have that brief summary of the Prosecution's position. I'll comment immediately on two of those points, then, and then come back to the question of the test. But on two of those points, secondly, the second point was that, well, essentially in a nutshell nothing has changed. There's no reason to depart from previous orders. What has changed is that it is the 28th of September, 2005, today, and it's as simple as that, that the question is: Where are we now? Not where we have been. Where we might have been is another issue perhaps that comes into play later. But it isn't a question of, well, what was the right thing for the Court to have done at some date in the past in the circumstances in the past? Of course there's an obligation to show some changed circumstances, but the changed circumstances are in effect the circumstances as we have them today, and that's the basis on which we proceed. The third point that was made, which is the acknowledgment in the motion of the accumulated backlog or deficit of $180.000 approximately in Mr. Krajisnik's contribution, and that is of course on the application of the Rules and requirements and directives, there is, as we said in the motion, there is no coherent legal or factual submission that we can make against that. The difficulty, as we have identified it in the motion, is that if it's said, well, $180.000 would -- of legal services would have enabled us to file a complete list of exhibits at this point, even if that's true, because we didn't have the $180.000. We haven't had those legal services. We are not in a position to do it. The trouble is, one can't change the real world. So we are presenting the Court very frankly with the real-world position. The real-world position according to the Rules of this Tribunal is there's an accumulated deficit of $180.000. Moving from that as, if you like, the real-world position for the purposes of this case, that means we might have had, if that money had been available, $180.000 worth of services, but we haven't. And that's the real world. And the real world, as we've indicated, is that we cannot and are not in a position to file the list of exhibits. So going back, then, to the observation that Your Honour made at the beginning of the morning. It no doubt was in some way an unpleasant surprise for the Trial Chamber to receive what is described as a fait accompli. The problem we have on the Defence side is that what we would have liked to be a fait accompli by the deadline was in fact a fait non accompli because we are not able, had not been able to do it. And the element of surprise there, Your Honours, with respect, has to be judged against the fact that I did make it crystal clear at the 65 ter discussions which led to the variation of the scheduled order that the Defence could not do this task before the 1st of October. And when pressed, I indicated that the 1st of October was a date before which we could not do it without my being able to say what date after the 1st of October was the date when we could do it, though I did make it clear that I wasn't talking about I think -- what I said was I'm not talking about the end of November or Christmas or anything like that, but I did make that plain, Your Honours. Now Your Honours didn't accept it in the sense that you did grant the extension by the order of the 26th of August, but accompanied it with recitals that the Trial Chamber had shown exceptional flexibility and with a specific recital that we had not in fact shown good cause. So it's not difficult to understand how a Trial Chamber that does not believe that good cause had been shown to vary the order but has nevertheless varied the order might, from its perspective, look upon what's happened perhaps as an unpleasant surprise. But the element of surprise must be severely qualified in the way that I've indicated. I should just mention, Your Honour, that in an attempt to be at least as helpful as we could in the circumstances, Your Honours will be aware, that we did notify the Trial Chamber on the Friday that the motion would be filed on the Monday. We just did not have time, with everything else, to complete it by the Friday. That has the slight advantage that we were able to bring the position bang up to date on the Monday. Your Honours, may I at this point just invite one piece of information, and it's something Your Honours haven't raised it yourselves, so may I, with respect, do so. We did at the end of our motion raise the question of the inaccuracy or incorrectness of a passage in the Trial Chamber's reasons for oral decision. Your Honours will be aware of that, where Your Honours had said that resources made available to the Defence team had increased or improved since the 24th of May. As we indicated in the motion, the Registry and we are agreed that that is wrong. Now, in the end, we are not the Judges. But may I, with respect, just invite the Trial Chamber to indicate whether it is accepted that that assertion in those reasons was wrong?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have to look to that exactly. I'll first have to reread it and to see what was exactly on our mind. I think it had something to do with the additional funding of investigators for, what was it, a thousand? Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm asking the question. If Your Honour throws back the question at me, I can't read Your Honour's mind, with respect. The difficulty here, Your Honour, is that I do, with respect, need an answer to this, because it's hampering my submissions. If I don't know what has been in the Trial Chamber's mind in relation to resources, which is, after all, a highly material issue here, especially --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I remember that there was an issue of the willingness of the Registrar to add, although limited, funds for investigations. It comes to my mind as I think it was $1.000 a month, but I'm not quite sure about the amount. And there was also a kind of an arrangement which would, as far as I understood, facilitate the replacement of co-counsel and that there would be some additional --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's absolutely wrong, with respect. Your Honour, this shows the enormous dangers. May I say, Your Honour, with the utmost respect, that that is an extremely woolly approach to an important issue. It is, Your Honour. It is vague, it is wrong, it's making assumptions in an extremely important area. It's quite clear that the Trial Chamber has all this material, inaccurate, incorrect, vague material, in its head, as some of the basis on which these decisions on scheduling are being made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me then ask you very precisely, Mr. Stewart: Is it true that the Registry has expressed its willingness to add to the amount available for the Defence, an, although limited, amount of money to be spent on investigators?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It is true, Your Honour, that the Registry finally, after about six months of negotiations, made an offer in a letter to me dated the 2nd of September, 2005, which was a week after the variation of the Scheduling Order, and some three or four months, and just on my feet doing the mental arithmetic, after the date Mr. Krajisnik expressed the wish to represent himself. The negotiations between the Registry and the Defence team, from the point where it was first indicated there might be some crack in the position up to February, that there would under no circumstances be any additional funding for the Krajisnik Defence team. The first crack appeared in February. Negotiations have continued ever since. They were not speeded up, I should say, Your Honour, they were not speeded up by the involvement of Mr. Krajisnik to produce tripartite or quadrapartite negotiations. They simply weren't. In fact, the opposite. And the culmination is what I've said, Your Honour, that on the 2nd of September an offer was made. It's a more complicated position there, Your Honour, but we met the Registry. Mr. Josse and I went to see the Registry yesterday. We had further discussions about that matter. But the simple position, Your Honour, is that no, no resources have been -- there has been no increase or improvement in resources since the 24th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If need be, we'll seek further information from the Registry, Mr. Stewart. I do understand that you say that there were no -- I was talking about willingness to give additional funding. You say this has not materialised until now, although I do understand that there's an offer, but I also understand from your words that, for whatever reason, whatever negotiations, situation, that offer has not yet been accepted, has not resulted yet in any additional funding.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that's -- yes, the last bit is -- it's slightly complicated, Your Honour, because there are questions of the old and the new Trial Chamber scheme. That way lies madness. We can explore it if necessary. But Your Honour, the nub of the point here is that what was said in that decision, which is unequivocally an assertion by the Trial Chamber that resources had increased or improved, is simply wrong, Your Honour. And the question of the transition or change of co-counsel, it is also absolutely correct that no additional resources were made available. Discussions and negotiations, and it did involve that, with the Registry in relation to the change of co-counsel proceeded on the insistence that it could be cost-neutral for the Registry, and with very considerable difficulty, I must say, Your Honour, and cooperation with all sort of people concerned, we were able to achieve that. It's not a trivial matter. May I say, Your Honour, Your Honour refers to inquiries made of the Registry. We have had, from the individuals specifically assigned to our case, we have had enormous help, which we appreciate in these discussions and negotiations from the specific individuals with whom we have day-to-day dealings, and we do appreciate that. Nevertheless, the whole process has taken a very long time. But one of the things that has troubled us, Your Honour, is also there was a reference in that same decision, the reasons for oral decision, et cetera, et cetera, there was a reference to a memorandum or a note which was sent by the Registry to the Trial Chamber which we, the Defence team, had not seen. And that's in principle an unsatisfactory situation when material is referred to expressly and taken into account for the purpose of the judgement without the Defence team even having seen it, let alone had the opportunity of making submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, it goes without saying that if the Chamber is provided with information which is not available to the Defence, I'm a bit more hesitant on the form in which it is presented, whether under all circumstances. But certainly preferable that the Defence would have seen the form in which it has been presented to the Chamber. That goes without saying. And if any mistake has been made in that respect, we'll certainly pay proper attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The essential point, Your Honour -- Your Honour said, well, in relation to the matter I just raised a moment ago that inquiries be made to the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I had in mind to invite the Registry to come to court and to explain the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would be 100 per cent satisfactory. That would deal with the obvious point, which was that everybody should know what is being said and taken into account and taken into consideration. The reference to that particular memorandum, which we have been supplied with by the Registry just recently, recently, I think it was some time last week, but I don't remember exactly. It might have been the week before, was referred to in paragraph 18 of that decision. So, Your Honour, that's the position. So far as the test is concerned, Mr. Tieger, but I suppose I should know what my own test is. Mr. Tieger didn't indicate precisely what test he was referring to. But I assume that he's referring to the criterion or criteria that we mention in our motion, particularly at paragraph 10 we start. But paragraph 9, the question whether the Defence are able to file any of what I've called the three components. And given that part of -- an important part of the reason for seeking an oral hearing, Your Honour, is so Mr. Krajisnik can understand what is going on. The three components are the list of witnesses required under 65 ter, the summaries, which is obviously closely linked, but it's a different item. It requires of course considerably different and extra work. And then thirdly, the list of exhibits. So those are the three components. And our submission was that the -- able to file the first question, leave aside responsibility and financial matters, the first simple question is whether the Defence are in fact able to file. Because no court, whatever its powers and its jurisdiction, can in fact make people do the impossible. They can make them try, but it can't make them do it. And the able to file, we submit and summarise, means able to file in a complete form and to a standard which leaves no significant deficiencies for the purpose of effect presentation of a defence to the charges of Mr. Krajisnik having regard to the gravity. And, Your Honour, because it is an issue which has arisen before, I do want to make it, please, crystal clear, that this is not a reversion by the Defence to some submission that perfect order is required or perfection is required in relation to submissions, or even that there is in this human world a perfection in the administration of justice. Because there isn't, and that's absolutely acknowledged. We are talking there about something which a standard which leaves no significant deficiencies. And we're talking about material deficiencies, which means that the stuff is simply not ready to file in a proper form which does the job. And we are talking about adequate. We are not talking about deluxe. Your Honour, the suggestion that the Defence has been able to adopt anything remotely approaching a deluxe standard in relation to anything at all in this case would be absolutely absurd in the circumstances. We don't do this. We are fighting all the time to achieve the bare minimum standard. And Your Honour, our submission in paragraph 11 of the motion, it may appear to have an element of defiance about it, but that isn't its purport. We say unless specifically directed to do so. But we must not, as counsel, file material on behalf of Mr. Krajisnik on these grave charges which is below that minimum adequate standard. It is our duty not to do that and to say we do not have the material ready to file. If one takes the extreme case, supposing we just have a rag-bag of scraps of paper with bits of notes on for 65 ter, well, it would be ridiculous, I suppose, if we've got to file those and those are supposed to constitute our 65 ter summaries. We're not in that position, Your Honour. We have worked hard on this. The updated number of 65 ter draft summaries which I'd indicated is a highly variable -- it's got a highly variable standard in it because they have been done by all sorts of different people on the Defence team. I'm not suggesting I do the best ones, but let's say that counsel would normally be expected to produce at the top end of the scale as far as quality is concerned. And it would be unfair and unreasonable to expect a very inexperienced intern fresh to the case with no practical experience to produce to the same quality as counsel. It would be pretty telling for both if that were the position. So it's a complete spectrum of material, and it does require, as we've indicated, considerable further attention from counsel. Now, Your Honour, what I would like to do is then turn straight to, in a sense, what, were those submissions about the standard, is the nub of the practical position as it is today, which is the point. And we have set that out, and we updated it last night to give the up-to-date figure on the number of draft 65 ter summaries prepared. We have given the Trial Chamber, and of course the Prosecution as well, our annex, which sets out in a really far more detailed, practical way than a team is normally expected to produce, but in the circumstances of this case, we see it as our duty to keep the Trial Chamber as fully informed as we can in relation to such matters. It does set out, as Your Honours can see, in some detail, where we have got to in terms of the amount of material and the timetable. And Your Honour, what I also do, with respect, issue as a, we say, legitimate invitation to the Trial Chamber, is this: That under the summary of the projected timetable for Defence work, we indicate, based on the material set out on four and a half pages of the annex, we indicate counsel days required. And we do submit that that is a sensible way of dealing with it, because the support staff, for all their manifest qualities, are that, the support staff work at every level has to feed into the work of counsel. Of course we delegate as much as we can, but in the end, the product has to be produced by counsel and submitted by counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I just ask one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you and Mr. Josse are working on a Monday, is that one counsel day or is that two counsel days?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Two counsel days, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, that's the unit. And I'm glad to be able to give that clarification. Yes, because, Your Honour, there might be a day that Mr. Josse has as his day off and another day that I have as my day off and so on. So that's clear. So, Your Honour, we calculate it. We do suggest that's a sensible unit to use. That's the key constraint on all final products on behalf of Mr. Krajisnik. And we do delegate, of course. Why wouldn't we? We're not crazy. Why wouldn't we delegate whatever we can, reasonably and safely delegate to the relatively small team we have, of course. What we have then done is we've given the total days available from now until the date of the 12th of October, is what we get to, in effect. It's a bit of chicken and egg. You do some figures, you lead to a date, and so on. But we've included all dates there. Seven days a week we included in what's totally available. We then subtract days which are needed for other things. And there, Your Honour, I would just issue this invitation: Your Honours have had the opportunity of reading this annex. Rather than my go through what might be the entirely time-wasting exercise of explaining or defending particular elements in that calculation, which are not in dispute, which are readily accepted by the Trial Chamber, by invitation is if there are any items, and Your Honours have had a chance to look at it, if there are any items in that calculation, if there are any elements in that subtraction about which the Trial Chamber has any questions, needs any clarification or has any significant doubts, then the most useful use of the remaining time that I have for the purpose of my submissions this morning is for me to have the opportunity of attempting to answer any such questions or doubts. That's an invitation there, Your Honour, because that is, in my submission, a reasonable, practical approach. We've set it out. Does anybody have any questions about it? Your Honour, may I add, just on a note: It was unconnected initially, but Your Honours know that I wrote, in effect, personally, but as counsel, but I wrote to Mr. Harhoff, with the intention that Mr. Harhoff should transmit the material to Your Honours, as he has done, and he and I had an informal word, I copied to the Prosecution a letter in relation to my own, and I do put it this way, but it is really strongly supported by those around me, my own need to have some sort of break from this case, which I have not been able to take over the last few months. Your Honour, the only -- I'm not going to elaborate that here this morning, but just to say, Your Honour, that this work on the annex was done after that letter, and what it has -- and they were not done together. They were not merged together in some deliberate way. The result of this annex just leads me to this, Your Honour: That I can see that the precise dates which I indicated in my letter could be potentially disproportionately disruptive in the light of what's set out in the annex. Therefore, Your Honour, I would be -- I hope Your Honours don't object to the tone in which I've put this. I would be prepared to defer those dates by one week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I must admit, Mr. Stewart, that the Chamber had some difficulties in reconciling what was in your letter, which was dated the 23rd of September, and from what I understand was received only by the 26th of September, with what we find in the motions that have been filed, especially the motion we are discussing now, on the 26th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm not following that. If you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The dates on when you thought you would not be available.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. It is for precisely that reason. It is that those documents were not prepared together. The letter about my break was written first, before reviewing in detail. I've now realised, having done this, that reviewing my letter in light of the annex, the specific dates I had in mind would be, as I've said, disproportionately disruptive. Therefore, I am suggesting I would adjust the date in my letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, in your letter you pointed at the week starting the 10th of October and the week starting the 17th of October, including the 24th of October, which is a UN holiday, so being available again on the 25th, from what I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Approximately two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- 24th, but that's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you now say is please understand that to be as everything moved one week.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour. It obviously makes sense from everybody's point of view that I incorporate that week when the Court has already indicated it's not sitting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But that -- so there's a long stop in a sense for two reasons. One, because if it goes any longer than a week's deferral, I don't get to incorporate that week; and secondly, Your Honour, quite frankly, I cannot keep going for that much longer. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At least it's clear to us now. And I wouldn't say that it resolves the problem, because we've -- we've spent quite some time to see how to reconcile your suggestions in your letter and the matters raised in the motion, and we might have to restart that. But please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. But I hope Your Honours at least see that whatever the content, at least see that actually giving the Trial Chamber notice and setting that out in my letter was intended constructively to give advance indication rather than simply spring something that is necessary. I should say, by the way, that whatever differences there might be, and there are from time to time, quite naturally, as in any case, between Mr. Krajisnik and myself, I do, with appreciation, acknowledge that Mr. Krajisnik himself is extremely understanding and supportive of such matters in relation to his Defence team, and he understands full well the need for conservation of energies for a marathon that is not a sprint, and I do wish to acknowledge that. So, Your Honour, that invitation -- because -- well, may I put it this way, Your Honour. The Defence would prefer not to hear points in a judgement which it might have been able to answer but was not asked to deal with and didn't have the opportunity of answering. So if there are any specific misgivings in relation to any of those elements which we have attempted to pare to the bare minimum, Your Honour, to cause the least disruption, then I would, with respect, like to know what they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber, Mr. Stewart, is hesitant to enter into the internal scheduling of the Defence. The Chamber is hesitant to give comments on this could be reasonably done in so much time, that should have priority, this -- I mean, that's all a matter for the Defence team itself to decide. And of course the Chamber has discussed these matters, and the Chamber avoids to enter into any debate on how the Chamber would consider that time could be saved on one element, more time would be needed on other elements. Because the Chamber would then interfere in what it considers to be entirely within the realm of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand that. The difficulty, with respect, is this: That when the Trial Chamber, and this is -- when the Trial Chamber will not accept assertions from counsel, if there isn't enough time, and the good-faith, professional assertion at the 65 ter conference, notwithstanding the variation of the schedule, was, in express terms, not accepted, because it was said that no good cause had been shown. Now, if the Trial Chamber at any point does not accept that assertion, and insists, as the Trial Chamber is doing, that the Defence gives fuller and more information in relation to the matter, then that information which we give does inevitably go into that normally private area of what our allocation of time is and what we do. If it is the Trial Chamber's position that it accepts that and accepts that that is a matter for us and that these items, as listed as subtractions are legitimate items, that they do require the time required and they do require them within this immediate short-term period, then that is an end of this issue. And I would then be entirely content, with respect, to endorse Your Honour's approach, that it is then left to us and the Trial Chamber does not in any way interfere. What I'm just concerned about is that the Trial Chamber then -- what I in a sense don't want to read and hear, Your Honour, is that in a judgement there is then some analysis of that, there is some criticism of that, there are adjustments made by the Trial Chamber when we haven't had a fair opportunity to answer the point. Because our position, Your Honour, is quite simple: All of these tasks have to be done. May I, for example, say: I know Your Honour is reluctant to answer questions, but we say surely the whole purpose of oral hearings and surely under this hybrid system, whatever else, part of the benefit of these oral hearings is to enable some exchange rather than everybody just standing up in turn and saying their piece with the Trial Chamber coming up at the very end. So are any of these items -- I do, with respect, repeat the question: Are there any of these items where there's any possibility that the Trial Chamber is going to say, No, we do not regard that as a legitimate expenditure of counsel's time, and therefore we are going to insist that that time is notionally, if you like, is actually, or for the purpose of calculating the schedule, notionally transferred to other work? Because if that is the position, it is a highly material point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since you have put the question for the second time and seemed to be not fully satisfied by the answer I gave, and I can tell you I gave it on behalf of the Chamber, even without consulting at this moment my colleagues, we will during the next break see whether the Chamber would consider to give any other answer than I gave already. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, that's an entirely fair and acceptable. I should say that straight away. Your Honour, there is a really serious issue at the heart of this motion. Are we to be compelled by a series of court orders and scheduling to do tasks which are counsel's tasks on behalf of Mr. Krajisnik inadequately because of the difficulties that we refer to in our motion, difficulties of funding, are we to be required to do that? Because the problem is, yes, some jobs can simply be done inadequately, in the sense that they can be done. We can file a batch of clearly inadequate 65 ter summaries that have not been properly considered and not been properly reviewed. We can file a list of witnesses which is not a properly, fully, adequately considered list of witnesses. In the end, yes, we can do it. I should say, Your Honour, we couldn't do it this afternoon or tomorrow or this week. We could file something -- list of exhibits is a real problem, Your Honour. We could file something that looks like a list of witnesses, that feels like a list of witnesses. We can file something that looks like a pile of 65 ter summaries and feels like and reads like a pile of 65 ter summaries. Yes, we can be compelled to do that, if a pre-emptory, or perhaps that's the wrong word, a very specific, absolute final direction is given that in a few days' time we should do that, yes, we can do it, if it is accepted that Mr. Krajisnik does not then receive an adequate defence. He is -- the deficiencies in his defence -- if the Trial Chamber wishes to say the deficiencies in Mr. Krajisnik's defence are his own fault, that inadequacy of funding is the explanation, well, that's the way in which we'll have to proceed. It's the Defence's submission that this trial has largely been conducted on that basis, not expressly acknowledged anyway, but has largely been conducted on that basis anyway. If that is the way we are to continue, then we submit that it really ought to be clear so that everybody knows where they are. But if what this Trial Chamber is requiring from counsel is something which meets the minimum, adequate requirement for effective assistance of counsel to produce an effective defence in this case, then this is the minimum time that is needed for this stage of the proceedings. And that issue really has at this point in this trial, that issue has to be faced head on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Mr. Tieger, have the observations made by Mr. Stewart triggered any need to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I believe so. Just a couple of points in response to Mr. Stewart's comments. First, Mr. Stewart noted the Prosecution's comments about the absence of the $180.000 of funding, and I believe dismissed the impact of the failure to provide funding by simply noting that indeed things might have been different but the Court has to simply deal with the reality of things as they currently are. With respect, I think that circumvents the question of accountability and responsibility for existence of that situation, and we submit that the accused cannot take action that should not be taken or fail to take action that he's required to take and then be heard to complain about the consequences of that action or that failure to act. I should also respond to the Defence's comments about my earlier reference to the Court's previous determinations on motions to adjourn or to extend the time. Again, I think Mr. Stewart focussed on an alleged distinction between where we might be and where we are now. The Prosecution's point, and that related again to the standard set out by Mr. Stewart, is that the focus is not necessarily -- the focus of the Defence test is not necessarily placed properly. So the Defence test, insofar as I'm able to understand it - and again I emphasise that I don't see a reference to any particular jurisprudential basis for that - is that we now find ourselves at the point he describes or that is described by the Defence motion in paragraph 10, that is, whether the case is now at a point where significant deficiencies exist, and so on. I believe that in the previous motions, as reflected in the Trial Chamber's earlier judgement, as reflected in the judgement by the Court of Appeal in respect to this particular motion and as reflected in a battery of reasonably similar motions made in a number of other cases, the question is broader than that, and that is whether or not sufficient time or adequate time has been -- and resources have been accorded the Defence in order to prepare an adequate defence. And there are repeated references to that much broader test, whether or not sufficient time and resources have been allotted to permit a reasonable defence. So the focus is not simply on where we are now, but what the broader situation is and has been. That's what we'd focus the Court on. And our reference to the earlier determination by the Court was that the same considerations were raised with respect to the same issue, and the Court addressed those. We submit both retrospectively when the motion was made, and obviously prospectively in the context of the case. And we think that's the basis on which the Court needs to make its determination. That test, I believe, also embraces the Defence argument that the Court hasn't accepted its good-faith assertion about time. Again, the test is not the subjective determination of either party, but the question of whether objectively sufficient time and resources have been allocated for the preparation of an adequate defence. And in that respect, we do submit then the Court's previous determinations bear significantly on the motion that is before the Court today. Finally, Your Honour, we would simply note this: That whatever decision the Court makes and whatever point is selected for the re-institution of this case, the Prosecution is entitled, under Rule 73 ter, to the full list of exhibits and to the full list of 65 ter summaries. And within a sufficient period of time before the recommencement of the case, so that we can deal with those appropriately. We would note that in the earlier portion of the case, to the best of my recollection, the Prosecution was required to submit those at least two weeks in advance of the hearing -- of the date on which the particular -- on the commencement of our case, far beyond that, and then any modifications of that were required at least two weeks in advance of the individual witness appearing. So we would request, as we have on earlier occasions, to have the complete list of the 65 ter summaries and of the exhibits. Nevertheless, it does seem to me that there is no contradiction in asking the Defence to submit whatever 65 ter summaries currently exist and whatever exhibit list it currently has, so that the review process can begin as soon as possible. That doesn't undercut our entitlement to the entire list, but there's certainly no reason not to get started on that process as quickly as we can. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I cite three short passages from the appeal decision on the interlocutory appeal on our second Defence motion for an adjournment. This was the decision of the Appeals Chamber of the 25th of April this year. Paragraph 2, at page 2 -- page 2 of the printout. It's paragraph 2, anyway: "In rendering the impugned decision, the Trial Chamber stated that it would continue to monitor the state of the accused's defence to" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I'll do that again, Your Honour. I was too fast. "In rendering the impugned decision the Trial Chamber stated that it would 'continue to monitor the state of the accused's defence to ensure a fair trial'." That's a general statement. It's just -- this is intended in response to the submission that all we've really got to do, unless -- and I suggest this isn't an unfair summary -- all we've really got to do is look back at the past decisions made by the Trial Chamber and nothing has changed. The second passage is at page 23, where the Appeals Chamber said: "It" - that's the Trial Chamber - "reasonably found that adequate time had been allowed for preparation of cross-examination of witnesses, and that in other areas, the Krajisnik Defence would have sufficient time during preparation of the Defence case, and in the presentation of it, to prepare adequately." Well, so we would have sufficient time during preparation of the Defence case, which is clearly distinguished from the presentation of it, so clearly you, the Trial Chamber, and the Appeals Chamber there, were clearly referring to the point before the first witness was called in referring to preparation of the Defence case. So what we're looking at now is whether we have had and are having adequate time during the preparation of the Defence case. And Your Honour, without belabouring the arithmetic, we looked at it on the 65 ter, the time given between the closing of the Prosecution case and the beginning of the Defence case, the original time proposed by this Trial Chamber was severely less than what had been contemplated previously. And then the third passage, at page 7, paragraph 29, in relation to strategy: "A Defence strategy can also be expected to be developed and refined in light of the case presented by the Prosecution as that case unfolds. Accordingly, if the Defence has not had sufficient time at this juncture to prepare an adequate strategy, it should allocate its available time to that task prior to the presentation of its own case when it has the benefit of having heard the Prosecution case in its entirety." Well, Your Honour, we had the benefit of hearing the Prosecution case in its entirety on the 22nd of July. By that time, co-counsel at the time was already, and I mean it metaphorically, dead on her feet, and had been for a little while. The time that we have had available to do that task - that's the strategy task - has to be combined with every other task, has to be combined with these tasks. And what I'm saying here, Your Honour, is just that it is absolutely compellingly incumbent upon the Trial Chamber not simply to turn back to those earlier decisions which were dealing with other aspects of the case at another time in other circumstances, and it's incumbent, heavily incumbent upon the Trial Chamber to meet its own commitment in the first of those passages, to keep the matter under review and look at the position as it is. The problem, if you like, or the issue which Mr. Tieger raises in relation to -- perhaps I should just comment on this, Your Honour, in relation to what I said about co-counsel, which had broader application to the whole team, but co-counsel naturally had to bear a very heavy burden. Counsel does bear the brunt of cross-examination. And Your Honours can look back at the period from February the 28th, when we reviewed -- resumed the case, and then, in particular, the period May, June, and July. And the programme of this case was, by any standards, absolutely punishing. And what I've said about co-counsel does have -- she's no longer with the case, but does have application to the whole team. Of course I had to impose very heavy demands on my co-counsel at that time, and I acknowledge that, in order just to get through the programme of this case. And what has happened since the 22nd of July can only fairly be assessed in the light of what was imposed upon this Defence team, and particularly counsel. Because it wouldn't have mattered if we had had $1.8 million to spend on support staff. If we've only got two counsel, then two counsel would have had to do and meet the schedule and deal with that punishing period. And it was two counsel. And it's a red herring if anybody suggests that effectively there were three counsel. That's not to disparage Mr. Josse's enormous contribution. Now he is co-counsel. But during that period. Because for practical purposes there were two of us, notwithstanding Mr. Josse's involvement occasionally at the very end of the Prosecution case. So that's where we are. In relation to what Mr. Tieger says about the filing of list of exhibits: Without necessarily accepting that there shouldn't be some exceptional flexibility shown somewhere in relation to that matter, we acknowledge that that is the prima facie position, that under the Rules as they stand, yes, that is the starting requirement and entitlement of the Prosecution, unless there are good reasons for some departure that they should have the entire list of exhibits. That's part of the problem, Your Honour, because the 65 ter material, the three components, really should be filed as a package, all of them done adequately. If there is some way. And we would be more than happy to enter into a constructive procedural discussion to see whether there is some way round the problems in relation to the list of exhibits which would be fair to the Prosecution, which would satisfy the Trial Chamber, and which would be practically achievable by the Defence. Well, we'll happily enter into such discussions. But if it is that all three components have got to be filed and then the 73 ter matters contemplate and from a sensible point of view can only be considered in the light of at least something which resembles a proper 65 filing of -- proper filing of 65 ter required materials, whatever qualifications or adjustments might be made in relation to the last of those components. Your Honour, it's back to really where I started. We can attempt the impossible, but we can't do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to have further information on the issue of the outstanding offer and what additional funds -- I'm not talking about the Chamber did not have at that time in mind that funding was fundamentally changed, but at least it was, I think, talking about some additional funds. I'm just confirming with the legal officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will adjourn for five minutes. Then, most likely, a representative of the Registry will be available to give us specific further information. That should not take that much time, if there's any need to comment on it, but I take it that the Registry will inform us according to the facts. And the Chamber is --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We're going to do that in Court, Your Honour, as I understood Your Honour's remark earlier on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But we'll take a five minutes' break for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then after that, we'd conclude the oral argument on this motion. The Chamber will then deal with the Davidovic issue briefly. The Chamber will also deal, as promised before, with the letter sent by Mr. Krajisnik, of which I do now understand that you have received a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That surprises me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- looking mystified, because I personally have seen such a thing, but my team is my team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be some confusion. When I'm talking about the letter, I'm talking about the letter Mr. Krajisnik has sent to us on the matter of that he wishes to appeal our decision on representation, not the letter sent to the Appeals Chamber. As a matter of fact, the letter which I was informed was sent to the Appeals Chamber, this Chamber has not seen it. And there is at least some reluctance to have a look at it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We have not seen any of the material, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the first letter, that is then really a mistake. The letter of -- I think it was the letter of 7th of September, which should then immediately - and there seems to be a misunderstanding - should be immediately given to you in translation in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think our position is that anything that this Trial Chamber has viewed, we would like to view as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that's the letter that we have viewed. So it will be provided to you. We'll adjourn for five minutes. --- Break taken at 12.11 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has invited Mr. van de Vliet to clarify the issue that was raised before the break. Mr. van de Vliet, there was some discussion about whether the additional funds, although limited, are available to the accused.
