What is in my recollection is that the Registry at that time expressed willingness to pay an additional $1.000 a month for the costs involved with further investigations in the preparation of the case against Mr. Krajisnik. Also at that time there was some talk about some overlap in the replacement of co-counsel. Could you inform us to what extent this has resulted in any financial means made available to the Defence of Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN DE VLIET
utterances.text: For sure, Your Honour. Just to give you a little overview of the recollection I have so available on such short notice, we have had discussions with the Defence team starting around March, involving the Registry and the deputy Registrar, to discuss additional funding to be provided to the Defence team under certain conditions. The amount that we discussed at that time was an additional $10.000 a month. And the conditions were related to the composition of the team and to -- involved in that discussion was also the possible replacement of co-counsel. The discussions were not finalised at that time. The matter of replacement of co-counsel was protracted, became a longer-lasting matter. And we have only concluded the discussions actually around this time, in September. What also happened in the meantime was the matter of self-representation by Mr. Krajisnik, which was delaying the finalisation of these discussions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That matter has been decided, as you know, Mr. van de Vliet. You are talking about an additional 10.000 a month. That's different from the amount of 1.000 a month for costs related to investigations and investigators?

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN DE VLIET
utterances.text: Yes. The idea of the 10.000 a month, which, by the way, by now has changed into 6.000. This is our final proposal. The proposal of the Registry that's on the table right now at this moment was not only to allow for investigations to be extended, but also to allow for three counsel to be operating in this team, which would allow for Ms. Loukas at that time to continue as a co-counsel. And we all thought that this would strengthen the team substantially and keep institutional knowledge on board. That was one of the conditions which was discussed at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you explain to us exactly what the present situation is. You said the discussions or negotiations were concluded around this time. Where do we stand? And could you also inform us whether, if there's any offer, whether it would have any retroactive effect. For example, if we are talking about the costs of investigations, whether if that offer would be accepted, that we'd start on the 1st of October or whether it would have any retroactive effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN DE VLIET
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. The situation is as follows: We will apply the new -- there has been a change in the policy for payments in the trial stage. We are going to apply that amended policy as of the beginning of the Defence stage, at the end of the Prosecution stage. This will allow for an additional $3.000 a month. That is as of the -- I think the 23rd of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN DE VLIET
utterances.text: That is in addition to what was provided before. Then what we also have offered, in addition to that, is what I just mentioned, an additional $6.000 a month to be spent on support staff, and we've laid out a few conditions related to those additional $6.000 to be spent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you give us any prediction -- perhaps I should ask that to Mr. Stewart, whether this last offer will be accepted. And if not, what would be the reasons not to accept what seems to be at least some additional funding?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I decline to conduct negotiations on this in open court. That simply is not the right course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Are the Registry and the -- nevertheless, Mr. Stewart, we are confronted with a situation in which you say, We don't get any extra money. We now receive the information by Mr. van de Vliet, who says: I made an offer, and it includes so and so and so much. And for the Chamber, we are talking about time and facilities available to the Defence. I'm not inviting you to enter into any further negotiations, but at the same time, if - and this is just one of the possibilities - for reasons which are not well understandable, an offer would be denied, then of course the Chamber has to ask itself whether these funds are available or not. If the Registrar would add any unreasonable conditions to it, the Chamber might come to the conclusion that these funds are not available. If, however, the conditions put by the Registrar are reasonable, but, for whatever reasons, for example, in the expectation or the hope to get more, if the conditions would not be accepted, if, for any reason, these available funds would not be accepted by the Defence, the Chamber might come to a different conclusion and come to the conclusion that the funds are available but have not been accepted. I do not invite you to enter into any further negotiations. If you say, I'd rather not express myself, then the Chamber will invite the Registrar to have a look at the conditions. I take it that they have been put in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN DE VLIET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise to interject, but maybe it saves time. Your Honour, I didn't say and I'm not saying that I'm unwilling to enter into further negotiations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In public, you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I said I decline to do it in open court. I'd like to add this, if I may, Your Honour: It's very clear from the most recent communication, as Mr. van de Vliet and Mr. Lowery will know, there was an e-mail from me this morning. We had, and I do say this, Mr. van de Vliet, it's usually the four of us recently, Mr. van de Vliet, Mr. Lowery, Mr. Josse and I, we do have very constructive, friendly discussions, and negotiations are clearly not finished, but they must be conducted in private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. But they are now conducted for six months and the issue --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we wish to analyse why it's taken six months, I'm happy to enter into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. You're not invited to do that. The only thing I say --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Would Your Honour please disregard a point like that in any judgement you reach if I'm not being invited to say anything more on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing to say is that the Chamber might not be able to afford to wait another six months and just to decide matters as they stand at this moment, you criticised our decision --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Correctly, Your Honour, because it's quite clear that your decision is wrong on that point, and nothing that's been said this morning alters the factual error in the Court's judgement. That is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What exactly, then, Mr. Stewart, is wrong in the decision? Could you please read the lines we --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "Resources made available by the Registrar to the Defence, as well as the composition and organisation of the Defence team, have increased or improved, also in the accused's estimation, since the accused raised the issue of self-representation on the 24th of May." Your Honour, it is absolutely plain still from what Mr. van de Vliet -- I don't -- there's more to be said, but I don't disagree with what Mr. van de Vliet has said at all this morning. I should make that clear. But it is simply not correct to say that resources have increased or improved. They have not. Mr. van de Vliet does not say they have, and he and I are in agreement on what he just said as far as it goes just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends on how you interpret the word "made available."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, "have increased or improved." Your Honour, we can leave aside the interpretation of the words -- I certainly, Your Honour, if necessary, would enter in submissions on the construction of the words "made available," but "have increased or improved," it is unambiguous, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What has been increased?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours' own judgement says: "Resources made available" -- yes, I agree, "made available." Your Honour, I do submit that that is reading something into that paragraph which it won't reasonably bear. It's perfectly plain that what the Trial Chamber was saying was that we had actually had more resources available to us, and that is clearly wrong. Your Honour -- with respect, Your Honour, the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- by not acknowledging--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- its own error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart. The only thing I said is that it may depend on how you interpret. That's the only thing I said. I leave it at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I ask this question: Is Your Honour saying that it was no part of your reasoning and no part of your decision and no part of your factual supposition that there had in fact been an increase of resources for the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the decision speaks for itself. If it's not clear to you, it's not for the Chamber to give any further explanations at this moment on its own decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, it is, because if there is ambiguity in a court's decision then it is the court which produced that -- it is for the court which produced that decision to resolve the ambiguity. There are limits to how far, as I indicated earlier this morning, anybody has or to presume to read Your Honours' minds. If it is not clear, it is for the court to resolve that lack of clarity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the Court is not going to give any further explanation at this moment. Is there any comment on the present situation as far as presented by Mr. van de Vliet?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I wish to say that what Mr. van de Vliet says, as I emphasise, is absolutely correct as far as it goes. And he was just invited, in effect, to answer specific questions. Well, one small point, Your Honour. It perhaps doesn't affect the price of fish very much, when Mr. van de Vliet said the discussions started in March, my recollection is that they started in February. But neither of us is working from notes this morning, so that's easily checkable. But it is true that at that time, $10.000 was under discussion, and Mr. van de Vliet says, and I fairly accept, that it was not offered at that point. It was subject to all sorts of matters and conditions which were under discussion. And we have discussed them. And they are -- there's a lot of complication in it. It's not useful to analyse this morning whether it could have gone more quickly and how it should have gone more quickly, because it's been very much at the heart of my submissions today that the most productive thing is to look at where we are actually on the 28th of September, 2005. And where we are is that, as I indicated, by Mr. van de Vliet's letter to me on the 2nd of September, an offer was made. And that, and I believe that is entirely agreed between us, that was the first time that an offer was made, as opposed to something which was still under negotiation in some form or another. The $1.000 of possible costs for investigators was in fact an element of the negotiations, particularly the bit of the negotiations between the Registry and Mr. Krajisnik. Of course, I became involved in that because they were -- in a sense they were tripartite negotiations, Mr. Krajisnik, the Registry, and me, with a sort of fourth party, the Trial Chamber, steering the negotiations and being informed and being involved in one way or another. So it's sort of three and a half parties, in a way. But that element was part of that. That was not, in fact, and there's no secret about that, that wasn't acceptable to Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Krajisnik and the Registry never were able to reach agreement on that. And on that particular issue, I'm largely not very far away, but I'm largely sitting on the sidelines on that particular issue, seeing whether the Registry and Mr. Krajisnik could agree, which they couldn't. I'm not far away on the sidelines. I'm pretty close to all of it. So that's the position as far as that goes. The six months, Your Honour, have of course gone by while we've been negotiating, without any increase in funding. I'm going to leave aside, Your Honour, because I don't believe that anybody is putting this as a big element in the equation, that sometime before the 24th of March, we were given and have been given 1.000 Euro a month, which is part of the new current scheme package. We have been given that for interpretation and translation costs between client and counsel. And that has been an increase in resources since earlier this year, but that dates back to before the 24th May. So I should just put that on the record. But otherwise, Your Honour, the three-counsel position was this: That actually, when we were talking about figures which involved for a long time involved $10.000, without the Registry, and I do acknowledge without the Registry ever having said to us, Yes, the offer is $10.000, when we were talking about that and we were looking at the figures, and there's been a lot of toing and froing, it seemed that there might be the opportunity to enable Ms. Loukas to stay in the case as, effectively, half a counsel. I don't mean she's only half a counsel. She's a complete counsel, but only half her time. Because Your Honours will be aware --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just as half a counsel as the Chamber is half a party.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, half a counsel is better than none, usually. Your Honours know that Ms. Loukas had not wanted to be a full counsel on this case for a very, very long time. It seemed that the opportunity might be there to use the funding so as to provide as one element of the, if you like, the new team package, two and a half counsel. Your Honour, that wasn't possible in the end. It wasn't effectively rejected by anybody. That's one way of looking at it, perhaps. But it just wasn't possible, Your Honour, with everybody doing their best in the circumstances. After all, if that half counsel had to be anybody, it had to be Ms. Loukas. There's no point in having half a counsel who was anybody else; it was to use her knowledge of the case. But it just wasn't -- it wasn't possible in the end, Your Honour. And in any case, Ms. Loukas wouldn't have been available for -- she wouldn't have been available straight off from the 23rd of July for three weeks, because she had made it clear for a long time that she was simply stopping and going away during that period. So the period we worked on this, it wouldn't have been possibly. That's water under the bridge. Your Honour, we are in a position now - Mr. van de Vliet and Mr. Lowery know this - one important additional element of the team which we have all talked about is to have a further legal assistant who speaks both English and B/C/S. We are in a position to implement that, well, we hope very soon, and in fact what's happened is before court this morning, among a number of other tasks, I sent an application, I sent it to Mr. Lowery, which is the right channel, so far as we understand, I sent it to Mr. Lowery for approval of a particular person who I mentioned to Mr. Lowery and Mr. van de Vliet in discussions yesterday, and we would hope that that could be implemented, well, I mean, as soon as the machinery can be done. But, Your Honour, what I want to stress, please, here is that it has not been possible and it would not have been possible, even if I had said to the Registry the second I'd received Mr. van de Vliet's letter, done deal, with all the conditions. There's lots else in the letter that does need to be sorted out one way or the other. But if I had said done deal as of today, it still wouldn't have helped us to any significant degree in relation to this immediate task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The issue we discussed, Mr. Stewart, was whether additional funds are available and whether the Chamber made any mistake in the language it used in its decision that the available funds -- the resources made available had been increased. That was the issue we discussed. And I think that we are now going far further, and there's no need, because I do understand that accepting the offer is not without difficulties. Let me say it very -- the Chamber would very much like to be informed about the conditions that accompanied the offer, and the Chamber would like to be informed, once the offer has either, with other conditions, yes or no, has been accepted or not, so whether finally the new funding scheme is put into practice, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Two things on that, Your Honour. First of all, yes, perhaps it would help, Your Honour, if I say that despite the slightly raised temperature submissions and discussion we've had in relation to that passage, if I contributed unnecessarily to raising of temperature, then I apologise. It is essentially water under the bridge. Because I am not appealing on Mr. Krajisnik's behalf the self-representation decision, whatever he at the moment is doing. So as long as for the purposes of these decisions that Your Honours are faced with today, as long as Your Honours are very clear that we have not actually had the benefit of increase of resources up to now, then no harm is done. I was simply concerned that that -- if there was a misunderstanding and error in that passage, it should not persist and be carried forward into these decisions. And, Your Honour, the position now appears to be very clear. Your Honours, with respect, do appear very clearly to understand that there hasn't in fact been an increase in resources. And that's adequate for present purposes. So far as the other element is concerned, Your Honour, it would not be the Defence's position that the Trial Chamber shouldn't be kept suitably informed of significant steps in the progress of such negotiations, and certainly it would be our position that the Trial Chamber should be informed of the results. What is important, and it links in with what has been said in other areas this morning, is that we should be informed of what the Trial Chamber has been informed about and that there should be no gap or uncertainty or lack of clarity as to what information the Trial Chamber has on anything, in fact. It's a wider principle in relation to this case. So that we know exactly what information the Trial Chamber has and exactly what it is taking into consideration. Apart from anything else, it gives the opportunity of correcting any misapprehensions or misunderstandings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, if any mistake was made in that respect in the past, it has to be deplored. Everyone is invited, first of all, I made it clear that we invited Mr. van de Vliet here in court so that there could be no problem in that respect. If there's ever any communication to be addressed to the Chamber which is of any relevance for either Prosecution or Defence, the Chamber will not accept such communications. And of course for practical reasons, now and then we have e-mail communications with the legal officers. It will not be accepted unless a copy has been sent to the interested party.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm very happy to hear that. I suppose for these purposes the Prosecution and the Defence would probably both always be interested parties in relation to anything of any significance. But, Your Honour, I'm very happy to hear that. And of course it has implications -- or it has application to some of the other matters we discussed this morning. Well, Your Honour, that is the position. Mr. van de Vliet, I also completely agree with Mr. van de Vliet in relation to -- because it's entirely consistent with what we discussed yesterday, that the idea is that the new scheme would have retrospective operation from the 23rd of July. That's been very fairly and clearly discussed between Mr. van de Vliet and Mr. Lowery and us. But Your Honours will appreciate that we can't -- our work can't have retrospective effect. We've only been able to do what we have been able to do with the resources we have actually had. We can only do from this point on what we can do with the resources that we will have. We hope this new member of the team will come on board very soon, but he won't realistically come on board to be able to help, apart from anything else, a new member of the team is of course an inevitable immediate call on management resources. You have to spend some time when you have a significant new member of the team. So, Your Honour, that's all I have to say. Do I understand -- or perhaps the question of the invitation I put to the Trial Chamber in relation to any questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered the matter. The Chamber has considered the matter and will not put any further question, which does not, as may be clear to you, automatically mean that the Chamber accepts everything. Because it's not for the Chamber to dive any further in how to spend time, resources, what should have priority, what could be done quicker, or what would even need more time than you suggested yourself. The Chamber is not going to enter into that matter, and the Chamber, therefore, has no further questions, which does not automatically mean that the overall assessment is accepted by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It does mean this, Your Honour. It means that if the Chamber in any judgement does reject any of those points without having given the Defence a fair opportunity of dealing with that point, well, obviously if we haven't had a fair opportunity, that will be an unfair result. That's the significance of my invitation, not to have matters sprung on us in a judgement when we haven't been given a fair opportunity of meeting objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, Mr. Stewart, you will also understand that the Trial Chamber does not want to take the role of an auditor for the projection of the work still to be performed by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do Your Honours understand, for example, why the end of stage report is of significance here and why time has to be allocated to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I explained to you that the Chamber will put no questions in that respect. This was not an invitation to check whether the Chamber understands everything correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's my function as counsel to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've done so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- to offer to fill in any gaps. That's part of my job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber has carefully looked at your submissions in this respect. Is there any further question for Mr. van de Vliet? I take it that the Prosecution has no specific interest to interfere in the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, we have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. van de Vliet, we thank you, and we'd like to see the conditions which accompany the offer as far as I understand that was issued on the 2nd of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN DE VLIET
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Your Honour. We will provide an overview of the past as well for your information. Could I add one more thing, please, just for the sake of clarity and completeness. It was our understanding yesterday when we met with both counsel that our offer was not going to be accepted. I understand now from the elaboration of Mr. Stewart that he would like to continue negotiation. If that is so, then we would be happy to have further discussions. But this was our understanding until this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If this hearing has added anything to the hope of reaching an agreement, we're only happy to hear that. If there is an agreement or if the offer is accepted or any other arrangement has been made, the Chamber would like to be informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can I just ask Your Honour whether, if I may do it through Your Honours, whether Mr. van de Vliet or Mr. Lowery have read my e-mail sent to Mr. van de Vliet and copied to Mr. Lowery at 8.02 this morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. van de Vliet, 8.02 this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN DE VLIET
utterances.text: Yes. I haven't read it at 8.02, but I have read it in the course of the morning, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, in that case, I'm sure Mr. van de Vliet didn't mean anything different. That does actually add something, and that does actually affect the position where we were at the end of the meeting. It does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I said, if we would have additional hope or better expectations to resolve the matter, it's nice to know that that's the situation. Mr. van de Vliet, I'd like to thank you very much for coming and informing the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Could I raise one further practical matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the presence of Mr. van de Vliet?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's a purely practical suggestion, that Your Honour was saying a moment ago, I think it's just scrolled off the screen, that the Court would like to receive some information from the Registry in relation to conditions. It occurs to me that the most helpful thing of all might be if Mr. van de Vliet and Mr. Lowery and we were able to agree a factual memorandum that we were all happy with to go to the Trial Chamber just summarising the position. Because we're not. I mean, we may disagree about where things lead. That's inherent in negotiations. But we don't disagree about facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If that could be provided to the Chamber still this afternoon, then it could replace the copy of the offer and the conditions attached to it. If not, the Chamber would like to receive the offer and the conditions attached to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is Your Honour saying that you have had the copy of the offer and the conditions attached?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. What I say is that we invited Mr. van de Vliet to provide us with a copy of the offer, but if by this afternoon another matter would be prepared for the Chamber, a memorandum which gives us the proper information supported by all involved parties, then that could come in place of -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It was probably just my misunderstanding of a particular remark that Your Honour had made. It was probably me, Your Honour. Thank you very much for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. van de Vliet, thank you very much. I do understand that -- thank you very much, Mr. van de Vliet. I do understand that the interpreters would prefer to have a break now. What is still on our agenda is, first of all, an oral guidance to be given to the Defence on certain matters that have been raised, which we have prepared and would be approximately one and a half pages of reading. There's also still a kind of a reaction or response, whatever you'd call it, to the letter of Mr. Krajisnik of the 7th of September. And there is the issue of Mr. Davidovic. First of all, let me establish: The Chamber considers that the oral argument on the motion for further extension of time is concluded. Yes. Then I'd like to hear from the interpreters whether they'd prefer to have a break now, which would be a break for some 20 minutes and then continue for another 25 minutes, or to start with the 25 minutes and then conclude for the day, hopefully in 20 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We'd rather continue right now, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'd rather continue. Then we have to ask whether the tapes allow us to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We would have, without any doubt, followed your preference to have a break now if so expressed. There is an issue that -- let me first briefly deal with the issue of Davidovic. Mr. Stewart, the last communication about it was that you thought that some time after the 3rd of October that you would be able to give a written reply from the Defence. I considered that to be linked, at least the 3rd of October, to the beginning of the presentation of the Defence case. That's what I had in mind when I talked about it earlier. I just wanted to briefly discuss whether you actually wanted to link the beginning of the Defence case. Because of course there's a fair chance that the presentation of Defence case will not start on the 3rd of October and whether we have to understand your message to be that shortly after or sometime after the beginning of the Defence case we could receive the Davidovic submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't think I wrote that -- I wrote that e-mail to the Trial Chamber, copied to the Prosecution, of course, I wrote that e-mail on the 14th of September. But as far as I recall, it wasn't an accident that it was the 3rd of October. That was indeed the date picked there because it was the beginning -- and it was for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber understands, then, your submission to be that sometime after the beginning of the presentation of the Defence case we'll hear from you. We'd rather not leave it too long, but on the other hand, it's a matter of principle rather than a matter of running urgently for a decision at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could I say, Your Honour, we don't wish to leave it any longer than -- can manage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's understood. Then the two issues the Chamber would like to raise. The first is what I would like to call the guidance on the conduct of the Defence case. This Chamber has been confronted on several occasions with the difficulties the Defence has had in finding a fair balance between the roles of Mr. Krajisnik and his counsel in conducting the Defence case. This concerns Mr. Krajisnik's involvement in the handling of courtroom proceedings and the choice of witnesses to be called for trial. It is not for the Chamber to find that balance. Nevertheless, as far as procedural consequences are concerned, the Chamber may assist the Defence in finding the balance. And to that end, the Chamber will provide certain guidelines that Mr. Krajisnik and his counsel are expected to follow in presenting the Defence case. First of all, the Chamber will address Mr. Krajisnik's repeated wish to put additional questions to witnesses. The Chamber exercises substantial discretion in regulating the conduct of the court proceedings and will allow Mr. Krajisnik a limited participation to complement examination-in-chief by his counsel. The Chamber will not fundamentally change the way the examination of witnesses has been conducted by the Defence and will extend the experimental phase when Mr. Krajisnik was allowed to participate in examining witnesses. The Chamber has no reason to doubt that the Defence counsel prepare the examination of witnesses, and in doing so, consult with Mr. Krajisnik in the usual way. After most of the time for examination has been used, Mr. Krajisnik will be given an opportunity to consult with his counsel regarding any remaining questions that, to Mr. Krajisnik's mind, have not been put to a witness. If the Defence counsel then do not ask such questions, the Chamber will positively consider whether to allow Mr. Krajisnik to put some questions to the witness, granted that Mr. Krajisnik demonstrates he is capable of putting his questions in a procedurally proper manner. The Chamber already expresses some concern on whether Mr. Krajisnik will fully understand the Rules applicable in examination-in-chief, whereas until now, Mr. Krajisnik has been asking questions only in cross-examination, cross-examining Prosecution witnesses. Therefore, the Chamber may at any time intervene and cut Mr. Krajisnik's examination short if the Chamber deems the examination to be disruptive or in violation of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Based on the experience the Chamber will gain in allowing this experimental examination mode, the Chamber may at a later stage consider whether or not to allow Mr. Krajisnik to continue to put additional questions to Defence witnesses. Finally, the Chamber needs to address the issue of the choice of witnesses. The Chamber again wishes to emphasise the need for mutual understanding and respect for the respective positions between Mr. Krajisnik and his counsel. This includes the choice of witnesses to be called for the Defence. Thus, the Chamber expects Mr. Krajisnik and his counsel to discuss the choice of witnesses and seek to reach a compromise whenever their views are not congruent. In case of disagreement, the counsel are expected to reconsider whether their opinion on the possibility of a witness not to further the Defence case outweighs Mr. Krajisnik's wish to make choices in what he considers to be the interests of his own defence. The counsel, however, are expected to warn Mr. Krajisnik about the possible detrimental effects of calling that witness upon their instructions. The Chamber recognises that a situation might arise in which the Defence counsel feel that the rules of ethics and professional conduct, by which they are bound, prevent them from following Mr. Krajisnik's instructions with regard to which witnesses should be called. If such a case should arise, and if Mr. Krajisnik has insurmountable difficulties in following his counsel's advice, the Chamber expects Mr. Krajisnik to address the Chamber directly during a court session, which means not in separate letters, and to indicate his wish to call a witness where his counsel feel that they are unable to follow. The Chamber will then consider Mr. Krajisnik's submission including the significance of the evidence and the subject matter of the testimony and may choose to call a witness as a Chamber witness. If this situation should ever arise, further instructions and guidance on the practicalities related to the examination of such witnesses will follow. As with the issue of putting questions to the witnesses, the experience the Chamber gains with the procedure may be of guidance regarding the continuation of this procedure in the future. That is the guidance the Chamber would like to give to the Defence in this respect. Then the last issue on the agenda --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I just raise a purely practical issue. We suggest it would be very helpful in relation to that passage, and it will be clear what it is, if the Court could arrange for that to be translated into B/C/S. Because that particular bit of the transcript, with all that guidance, is obviously important and useful for Mr. Krajisnik to have at his side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, first of all, there is, although it's only 99.5 per cent what I just said, we have it on paper in English already, but we'll see -- I mean, it's guidance. It's not a decision. So we'll see whether there's a possibility to have this translated and to be given to Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the last issue I'd like to raise is a -- well, whether it's a real response is another matter, but at least a reaction of the Chamber to Mr. Krajisnik's letter of the 7th of September, 2005. Because, Mr. Krajisnik, the Chamber would like to make some comments on the letter you have sent to us on the 7th of September, 2005. In that letter, you raised three issues. First, you suggested that the Chamber had agreed with your counsel to a timetable for the trial and that the deadlines envisaged in that timetable were too harsh for the Defence. Second, you expected confirmation that you had, and I quote your letter, "a right" to pose questions to witnesses, and I quote again, "in addition to the lawyers." Finally, you expressed your intention to appeal the Chamber's decision on self-representation of the 18th of August, 2005. I will not expand at this moment on the reasons you gave for this wish to appeal the decision. The Chamber clarifies that there was no agreement between Defence and Chamber on the schedule for the trial and that this issue is still pending due to the latest filings by your counsel. We confirm our intention to give this matter immediate and careful consideration. The issue of your involvement in the Defence strategy and of your limited possibility to ask questions was addressed just a few moments ago through our guidelines, or guidance. On the issue of your appeal, you sought information on deadlines to appeal the Chamber's decision and you asked to be provided additional legal assistance in this matter. Mr. Krajisnik, you have legal assistance. Mr. Josse, moreover, was in Court with you on the 19th of August, the day after our decision was filed. If you had consulted with your legal counsel, you would have found out that there are seven days to ask for certification to appeal against an interlocutory decision. You would also have found out, most likely, that no additional counsel would have been assigned to you on this matter. Finally, you would have been reminded that any motion or application must be filed with the Registry. Even if the Chamber would understand, which it does not, the letter as an application for certification, it was sent too late. It must have been clear to you that you were not unrepresented. However, it seems as if you were under the misapprehension that the time would be running only when you formally received a written translation of the decision. This is not so. Moreover, I recall that the Chamber made specific arrangements for you to receive a preliminary unofficial translation on the 19th of August, after our hearing on that same day. Your letter confirms to the Chamber your need to be represented by counsel. Dispute the fact that the letter, as such, does not require any decision, the Chamber has decided to respond to it in the way it does. The Chamber wishes to add that an accused, represented by counsel, should send a letter to the Chamber, its Judges, or its staff only in exceptional circumstances. Exceptional circumstances did not exist in this case, and the issue of an appeal should have been raised, in due time, through counsel. Yes, Mr. Krajisnik. The Chamber has responded to your letter. It does not envisage to have a debate, but we'll not deprive you from an opportunity to make some, although limited, observations. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for having responded to the letter I sent. I just wanted to offer a few sentences by way of clarification, trying to be as brief as possible. Your Honours, I don't want to be yet another case here or to interrupt the existing proceedings. I have restated on several occasions that I have great respect for this Trial Chamber and for the proceedings itself. One thing is clear, though: You have given us an opportunity to consult with Mr. Josse concerning your decision, but we had five minutes, at the most, because the guards had said that we had to leave urgently, and that could be confirmed by Mr. Josse. We couldn't converse then, and Mr. Josse didn't know what the deadline for the appeal was. The appeal itself is not a problem. I was encouraged to hear today that you have given deep thought to the essence of this issue. There is only one thing that I ask, and that is a fair trial, nothing more than that. I will be happy not to ask a single question. But I wanted to mention something that was stated here by the OTP, and it was incorrect, and concerns my participation in the trial. As I said, I want to participate in the expense of my defence up to the $180.000 that were mentioned, and I will prove that I had participated. This was mentioned as one of the main reasons here, and it was somewhat corrected by Mr. Stewart. I believe it was useful. Anything that should have went the way of the investigators, all those obligations were met. But the investigators put together a lot of material. They took the statements. But what is of essence here, and as Mr. Stewart explained, is that there was still the lack of resources for the attorneys. There are submissions to be made, and this was the part that Mr. Stewart discussed with the Registry. Therefore, it is not that I didn't want to meet my financial obligations. I do. As I said from the beginning, I do not -- agree with the decision, but I accept it. It's been a year now that the investigators haven't been paid. But I will come up with a way to compensate for their work. In addition to that, I would like to thank you for giving these extensive guidelines as to my relationship with the Defence. I am sufficiently intelligent to work in my own best interest and not contrary to it, but the problem is the lack of resources at Mr. Stewart's disposal. Another thing, if I may. On the 31st of August I received the decision on the appeal. I sent three letters to the Registry prior to that, asking for help, for assistance. It is true that I asked the Registry not to be given assistance from my team, my Defence team, and there was a certain conflict between us, since I was looking to find better ways for my defence, for the conducting of my defence. I was slightly worried, because I was afraid they wouldn't be able to do it in a quality way, due to the lack of resources. I am at the disposal to the OTP, to the Chamber, and I can document each single dollar that represented my financial obligations in these proceedings. I wanted to ask Mr. Stewart to say publicly whether he was ever refused by the investigators anything -- whether they have given all the documents when they went to Pale. If I may conclude, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, this is not an issue to be raised in this forum to ask public statements by counsel. If you want to address the matter, please discuss it with Mr. Stewart. Please proceed, if there's anything else you would like to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I would like to ask you the following: As for the Defence case and the evidence presented, I wanted to make clear that Mr. Josse and Mr. Stewart are doing their best to link all of the pieces of the puzzle. But what is important to me is that we end these proceedings as soon as possible. But they cannot. That's why I asked to be of help, not to be yet another attorney. Because the OTP is now using it, saying he is not able to do that. Quite the contrary; I just wanted to try to save time, in case we omitted something of crucial importance. So I would kindly ask for your understanding. I make my own notes, and I have a list of questions to be asked of all of the witnesses. Mr. Stewart can have his opinion on that, but I would like to ask him nonetheless. It is easy for you to interrupt me to make decisions, but I would kindly ask you for your understanding, for the truth's sake. I would kindly like to remind the Chamber, at least the Judges that were present at the time. From the beginning I would asking for one thing, to be able to prove the truth. But this is now the improvisation on the part of the Defence. That's why I wanted to ask for a quality defence and that the people who are truly guilty be brought before the Tribunal. That's why I wanted to appeal, to represent myself, to change the way my defence is being conducted. I still have great respect for the Chamber. Hence, I decided not to appeal further. I wanted to forward a request for certification for an appeal, since I am -- I have the right to represent myself. I would simply ask for your understanding to see my point, to help the entire proceedings. As for the Registry, I sent a letter to you once negotiations were completed. We dealt with the Registry concerning all of the technical matters, and the remaining issue was the one that you discussed today, as well as the $1.000. I agreed that the Chamber should make a decision on that and that everything else has been dealt with. But they didn't put basic preconditions in place for me. I have one room where I need to fit all of the papers and there is no room to breathe in it. Hence, I'd like to ask that the Registry meet its own obligations and that you exercise some understanding for Mr. Stewart's request. We may disagree on many matters, and even today there is tension between us, but I believe that the only way to conduct a good, solid defence is to have a good cooperation between the client and his Defence attorney. I would like to thank you yet again, and I will not abuse your time further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The matters that Mr. Krajisnik referred to on the 19th of April, I can broadly speak and confirm that he's right in both regards, for what it's worth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That doesn't change anything, apart from that the matter is moot anyhow, on the basis of -- but of course I take it that if Mr. Krajisnik would like to have discussed in due time and would have to be informed about what the time-limits were, that there would have been no difficulty, if not on the spot, then, well, within the time needed for that to be informed about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour will excuse me for not going into that. I simply wanted to confirm that was true. Mr. Krajisnik invited me to in the course of that submission. I felt I should. I didn't expect it to in any way change the view of the Trial Chamber. It's for information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The matter is moot anyhow, because Mr. Krajisnik informs us that he does not wish to continue the -- or to appeal. Mr. Krajisnik, you asked a lot of things from us. I'm going to conclude at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to contribute that the proceedings continue further. That's why I gave up my right to appeal. I would kindly ask for your understanding to provide assistance and to take Mr. Stewart's request into consideration, to come up with the optimum framework to begin with the trial in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you've raised quite a number of issues. Of course, the most important one is that you are asking for a fair trial, and it's the responsibility of this Trial Chamber that you will receive a fair trial. On any of the other matters, to some of them we've given you already the relevant information as to how to proceed and what your role, as far as the procedural consequences are, may be. If there's any specific matter, for example, you ask us to decide a certain matter for the Registrar, you're invited to consult with counsel to what extent what you'd like the Chamber to do is within the competence of the Chamber. And if it is in the competence of the Chamber, counsel will know how to address the matter in such a way that the Chamber will give decisions on issues raised. This concludes this hearing. The Chamber will consider the motion for further extension of time. We'll give a decision. And since we're also aware that we should not wait too long, we'll also try to see whether we can file a written decision today. I'm not giving any promises, but the parties are invited to check the possible filing, because whatever the Chamber may decide, it may have some time implications for both Defence and/or Prosecution. And the earlier you know about that, perhaps the better it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is it possible, because I assume that such decisions are done on a computer or word processor, is it possible for, once the decision is failed, for it to be e-mailed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Once the decision has been filed, I will invite the legal officers to send a copy, a courtesy copy, which is not binding the Chamber in whatever way. If you want to know what the decision is, you should check at the Registry. But I have sufficient confidence in our legal officers to assume that the same text will reach you by an e-mail as it is filed at the Registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Your Honour. That's very kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn, sine die.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: sine die

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.33 p.m.,
